hints: Look carefully at what Fig. 5.1 actually shows - do you see the outside surface of whole bacteria in 3D, or a thin slice through the inside of cells?
walkthrough:
Read the Image Like a Microscope**
Fig. 5.1 shows whole, rod-shaped bacteria with flagella standing out in 3D. You can see surface texture and depth, with some cells in front of others. That 3D surface view is the signature of a scanning electron microscope.

Contrast With the Other Type**
A transmission electron microscope sends electrons through a very thin section, so you would see a flat 2D slice showing internal ultrastructure like membranes and cytoplasm. Because this image shows external surfaces, not internal detail, it must be scanning.

hints: Recall the classic AS Level example of a curved rod-shaped bacterium with a flagellum that causes severe watery diarrhoea - what is its genus beginning with V?
walkthrough:
Link Disease to Pathogen**
Cholera is caused by a bacterium, not a virus. In the syllabus this is always the same species, a comma-shaped Gram-negative rod with a single polar flagellum, just as you can see in Fig. 5.1.

Write the Binomial Correctly**
The genus is Vibrio and the species is cholerae, so the full name is Vibrio cholerae. Remember to use italics or underlining if handwritten, with a capital V for the genus and lower-case c for the species.

hints: Work through the passage sentence by sentence - size $1-5 \mu m$, no double-membrane organelles, 70S ribosomes, circular DNA free in cytoplasm are all true, so focus on the polymer named for the cell wall.
walkthrough:
Check Each Statement**
Prokaryotes are indeed $1-5 \mu m$, unicellular, lack membrane-bound organelles, have 70S ribosomes and circular DNA free in the cytoplasm with no nuclear envelope. All of that is correct.

Spot the Plant Feature**
Cellulose is the wall polymer of plants and some algae, not bacteria. Prokaryotic walls are made of peptidoglycan, also called murein, a mesh of sugars cross-linked by short amino acid chains. So the error is cellulose cell wall, corrected to peptidoglycan cell wall.
Final answer: cell wall is not made of cellulose, it is made of peptidoglycan / murein
